lines: {target}? Vines can hide lava as well as stone.
If anyone heads for Jungle Ruined Portal, tell them. Clear the leaves before stepping close.
The jungle grows over Nether scars, but not kindly.
I would like to see Jungle Ruined Portal once, though I would bring plenty of blocks.
I will remember Jungle Ruined Portal as a green ruin with a red memory underneath.
Vines hide the shape of the frame and the holes around it. Clear them from a distance.
Wet leaves won't help if the netherrack beneath them catches.
I'd cut one clean path to the ruin and use the same path back.
Jungle roots can pry apart blocks that survived the portal itself.
A parrot going quiet may notice danger before we do.
Moss makes crying obsidian slick enough to throw a careless climber.
The canopy traps smoke low around the site. If the air stings, leave.
I wouldn't swing an axe near a lava pocket I couldn't see.
Water runs everywhere in a jungle, but not always where a fire starts.
A bright marker above the ferns would keep us from circling the ruin twice.
That chest may have vines growing through the lid. Let them be until the ground is checked.
I'd test the soil with a spare block before stepping across any dark patch.
Fallen logs can make a bridge over netherrack, though I'd rather use stone.
The jungle will cover this place again. That doesn't mean it becomes safe.
If something moved beyond the frame, the leaves would make a poor escape route.
{target}? Broken obsidian near cliffs makes bad footing worse.
If anyone heads for Mountain Ruined Portal, tell them. Mind the edge before minding the chest.
Thin air and Nether stone both make folk careless.
Your story makes me curious about Mountain Ruined Portal, though not careless.
I will remember Mountain Ruined Portal as a high ruin where one bad step travels far.
The portal isn't the worst danger if the ledge beneath it is coming loose.
Obsidian is strong, but it won't hold an entire scree slope in place.
I'd tie off before climbing down to any chest below the frame.
Snowmelt can run under the ruin and freeze again after dark.
A loose block on that ridge may travel all the way to the valley.
The wind can push smoke across the only safe approach without warning.
I'd build a short retaining wall before spending time near the portal.
Gold on a cliff is still gold on a cliff. It can wait.
The mountain gives us fewer ways out than the open country does.
A bright marker below the ridge would help if clouds swallowed the summit.
Don't shelter under the frame. Broken arches drop pieces when the ground shifts.
Blackstone steps ice over just as easily as ordinary stone.
If the ledge sounds hollow, crawl back toward the slope and spread your weight.
We should clear fallen netherrack from the trail before leading anyone else up.
I'd rather view that ruin from the next ridge than test the edge beside it.
{target}? A broken portal in the Nether still feels too awake.
If anyone heads for Nether Ruined Portal, tell them. Keep fire behind you and a way out ahead.
Obsidian there looks less broken than hungry.
I can see why people keep talking about Nether Ruined Portal after they leave.
I will remember Nether Ruined Portal as a ruin inside the place ruins come from.
A broken portal here may be the only landmark for a long way. Don't lose sight of it.
Blackstone blends into the ground until a crack opens red beneath your feet.
I'd wall off the lava before touching the chest, even if piglins were nowhere nearby.
Gold around a Nether ruin belongs to whoever is watching. Assume someone is.
There is no cool side to approach from, only a side with less fire.
A short cobblestone shelter could make the site useful without repairing the frame.
If the obsidian starts to glow, step away and count everyone.
Netherrack crumbles too easily for a loaded pack. Put weight on the blackstone.
I would leave arrows pointing toward the route home at every fork.
Ghast fire can turn a careful inspection into falling rubble.
The ruined frame may block one blast, but it also hides what stands behind it.
I'd keep one solid wall between the group and the nearest open drop.
A chest beside lava is bait for rushed hands. Let the ground cool first.
If we use the ruin as a landmark, nobody moves it for spare obsidian.
The Nether already has enough open doors. We don't need to mend this one.
{target}? Lava stone under water makes no honest sense.
If anyone heads for Ocean Ruined Portal, tell them. Watch your air and anything glowing below.
The sea should not know that much heat.
Your story makes me curious about Ocean Ruined Portal, though not careless.
I will remember Ocean Ruined Portal as a drowned portal still remembering fire.
Obsidian is easy to spot below clear water, but the current can carry you past it.
Magma beside the frame may drag a swimmer down before they reach the chest.
I'd place an air pocket above the ruin before exploring the lower blocks.
Crying obsidian looks different underwater. Follow the bubbles, not the shine.
A boat anchored directly over the site could become trapped on rising magma bubbles.
The seabed may be sand around one side and solid stone around the other.
Drowned can hide inside the frame where the water turns dark.
I would mark the surface with a buoy so the group doesn't drift apart.
Lava and seawater leave rough stone that can catch a boot or tear a line.
There is no sense opening a chest while your last breath is already leaving.
I'd block the magma flow only after checking where the bubbles give us air.
The portal ruin is sturdy enough to survive waves, not safe enough to trust blindly.
Keep the return rope clear of every obsidian corner.
If the weather turns, abandon the dive before the shoreline disappears.
Anything worth taking from the bottom will still be there after we prepare properly.
{target}? Mud, vines, and Nether stone all grab at your feet.
If anyone heads for Swamp Ruined Portal, tell them. Bring blocks and leave before the fog thickens.
Swamp water makes broken obsidian look sicker.
I have never been to Swamp Ruined Portal. Thanks for telling me about it.
I will remember Swamp Ruined Portal as a wet ruin with a fever under it.
Mud can swallow the bottom of a frame and leave the top looking level.
I'd lay a plank walk before carrying stone across that waterlogged ground.
Lily pads hide where the bank ends and the deep water begins.
The fog may cover smoke from a small fire until we are standing in it.
Swamp vines tug at packs when you need both hands for balance.
A foundation here needs pilings or broad footing. Loose mud won't hold a narrow wall.
I would keep the boat tied on the open-water side of the ruin.
Slimes make poor company when you're balancing near broken obsidian.
The chest could be half underwater, and the lid may open into nothing but roots.
Netherrack stays ugly even after years of rain and moss.
I'd mark firm ground with cobblestone so nobody follows a sinking trail.
A lava pocket in a swamp throws steam before it shows flame.
If the walkway starts bobbing, turn around one at a time.
The ruin may be old, but the mud around it changes after every storm.
We should be back in the boat before night creatures start using the fog.
{target}? Broken planks underwater snag the careless.
If anyone heads for Shipwreck, tell them. Count your air before counting loot.
The sea keeps what sinks unless you bargain well.
I know more about Shipwreck now than I did this morning.
I will remember Shipwreck as a drowned hull that still knows how to trap feet.
A hull on the seabed can shift when a current gets under the ribs.
I'd enter through the widest break instead of squeezing past rotten doors.
Air first, chest second. The order shouldn't need arguing.
Waterlogged planks hold together until someone pulls the wrong one free.
A drowned inside a cabin has every doorway in its favor.
I would tie a line from the mast to the boat before diving below deck.
Sand may have buried the lower hull and everything waiting beneath it.
The map room is not safe merely because sunlight reaches the windows.
Loose trapdoors can close behind a swimmer when the current changes.
I'd leave any beam that still supports the deck exactly where it is.
One dry door placed well can give us time to look around without panic.
If bubbles start thinning, follow the rope and forget what remains in the chest.
The stern often sits deeper than it appears from the surface.
A storm can move our boat while we're still inside the wreck.
Old cargo isn't worth becoming new cargo on the ocean floor.
{target}? A ship on land already lost one argument.
If anyone heads for Beached Shipwreck, tell them. Watch rotten planks and the sand under them.
Wood that survived the sea can still give way.
There is more to Beached Shipwreck than the maps suggest.
I will remember Beached Shipwreck as a stranded hull with old trouble in its ribs.
A stranded hull settles every time the tide softens the sand beneath it.
I'd prop the leaning side before walking through the lower cabin.
Dry planks can be more brittle than the soaked wood below the tide line.
A beached ship makes good shelter only after the broken ribs are checked.
The next high tide may reach farther into the hold than today's did.
Sand piled against the hull can hide doors, chests, and holes alike.
I would build steps to the deck instead of climbing a mast that already failed once.
Gulls are loud enough to hide the sound of a beam cracking.
The stern may look grounded while a hollow pocket sits beneath it.
A campfire belongs outside and downwind from all that dry timber.
We can salvage loose boards without pulling apart the frame that keeps the roof up.
I'd mark a safe path above the tide line before dusk.
If the hull groans when the waves return, nobody sleeps inside.
A chest under the sand can wait until the wall beside it is braced.
The ship lost its voyage, but it doesn't need to take a traveler with it.
{target}? Deep stone can lead farther than anyone planned.
If anyone heads for Stronghold, tell them. Mark every stair and do not stare too long at the portal room.
Silverfish turn old blocks into bad surprises.
You came back from Stronghold with a better tale than a scar.
I will remember Stronghold as a buried place asking questions in stone.
Before laying a single block at Stronghold, I would test the branching stone corridors twice.
Good corners matter more than decoration when building near the branching stone corridors.
I would brace the side nearest the branching stone corridors before anyone settled in.
Anything valuable at Stronghold can wait until the return route is safe.
I would leave one block marker at every turn between Stronghold and the last staircase toward daylight.
I would count the turns back from Stronghold while my legs were still fresh.
I would keep the tools packed at Stronghold until the group had a safe position.
I would choose the shelter site at Stronghold with doors leading in circles in mind.
At Stronghold, doors leading in circles would worry me more than anything worth carrying home.
I would look above the last staircase toward daylight as often as I looked down at my feet.
I would study the branching stone corridors before choosing where the group puts its weight.
At Stronghold, I would watch where loose pieces gather near the branching stone corridors. They show where people slip.
If you go to Stronghold, tell someone which marker you expect to reach first.
Do not split up at Stronghold just because the ground looks open.
I would share the load before asking anyone to hurry across the branching stone corridors.
{target}? Witches do not need much room to make trouble.
If anyone heads for Swamp Hut, tell them. Keep milk ready and do not breathe the potions.
A little hut can smell like a warning.
I wondered what Swamp Hut was really like. Now I have an answer.
I will remember Swamp Hut as a crooked house where bottles mean danger.
For Swamp Hut, I would carry rubble for fill and dressed stone for the places taking weight.
Before laying a single block at Swamp Hut, I would test the waterlogged ground around Swamp Hut twice.
For Swamp Hut, a low shelter makes sense when the main concern is mud hiding deep water.
At Swamp Hut, everyone should recognize the start of the firmest roots toward open land before the group spreads out.
Before exploring Swamp Hut, I would walk the firmest roots toward open land once in both directions.
If the light changed, I would still want the firmest roots toward open land easy to recognize.
At Swamp Hut, a shelter plan that ignores mud hiding deep water is not finished.
When the danger at Swamp Hut comes from mud hiding deep water, the nearest solid corner will matter.
I would keep the tools packed at Swamp Hut until the group had a safe position.
At Swamp Hut, I would trust the sound under my boots before the view ahead.
The safest-looking surface at Swamp Hut still deserves a careful step.
I would note every narrow point along the firmest roots toward open land at Swamp Hut. Tired feet find those places.
I would rather return empty-handed from Swamp Hut than leave someone alone near the waterlogged ground around Swamp Hut.
The possibility of a slime beyond the roots is reason enough to keep everyone near the firmest roots toward open land.
I would share the load before asking anyone to hurry across the waterlogged ground around Swamp Hut.
{target}? Old roads leave sharp bits behind.
If anyone heads for Trail Ruins, tell them. Brush carefully and do not dig like a fool.
The past breaks easily when rushed.
Your story makes Trail Ruins sound worth seeing with a careful group.
I will remember Trail Ruins as buried paths with history under the dirt.
One safe room at Trail Ruins is worth more than five hurried walls.
I would put the first solid corner at Trail Ruins where everyone can reach it.
For Trail Ruins, a low shelter makes sense when the main concern is gravel sliding into the dig.
If the light changed, I would still want the marked trail back easy to recognize.
No one should cross the hard part of Trail Ruins without agreeing on the way back.
The safest retreat from Trail Ruins should not depend on someone remembering the view.
Any camp at Trail Ruins needs to account for gravel sliding into the dig before nightfall.
When the danger at Trail Ruins comes from gravel sliding into the dig, the nearest solid corner will matter.
I would choose the shelter site at Trail Ruins with gravel sliding into the dig in mind.
The shape of the marked trail back matters as much as its length.
At Trail Ruins, a fresh scrape near the buried old road would tell me someone passed through recently.
I would note every narrow point along the marked trail back at Trail Ruins. Tired feet find those places.
Before dark at Trail Ruins, I would choose one meeting point and make it obvious.
Do not split up at Trail Ruins just because the ground looks open.
At Trail Ruins, the last person in line should know the plan as well as the first.
{target}? Rooms built for tests rarely grade kindly.
If anyone heads for Trial Chambers, tell them. Save strength for the next door, not the first cheer.
Copper halls can turn brave feet around.
Your story makes me curious about Trial Chambers, though not careless.
I will remember Trial Chambers as a place that measures courage by bruises.
I would keep the first shelter at Trial Chambers simple until we understood the site.
Stone for Trial Chambers needs rough faces for grip, not polished faces for show.
Before laying a single block at Trial Chambers, I would test the copper-lined rooms twice.
I would place a marker beside the last opened doorway before taking another step at Trial Chambers.
If we had to run, the last opened doorway should already be marked and open.
The safest retreat from Trial Chambers should not depend on someone remembering the view.
I would keep the tools packed at Trial Chambers until the group had a safe position.
If our plan did not account for traps changing without warning, I would call it unfinished.
A warning about traps changing without warning belongs at the first marker, not the last one.
At Trial Chambers, one loose block can explain a whole ruined wall.
At Trial Chambers, a fresh scrape near the copper-lined rooms would tell me someone passed through recently.
At Trial Chambers, a straight line of blocks could be a path, a wall, or a warning. I would find out which.
If you go to Trial Chambers, tell someone which marker you expect to reach first.
A missing tool is annoying. A missing traveler at Trial Chambers is worse.
Do not split up at Trial Chambers just because the ground looks open.
{target}? Neighbors there fight heat before anything else.
If anyone heads for Desert Village, tell them. Bring water and news, not trouble.
Sand gets into doors, beds, and tempers.
I would need a strong pair of boots before trying Desert Village myself.
I will remember Desert Village as another village trying to keep shade and hope.
Their sandstone walls keep rooms cool, but the flat roofs need checking after every hard wind.
A shaded well is the center of village life when the road runs through desert.
I'd bring spare slabs for awnings. Good shade is worth more than decoration there.
Sand piling against a door can trap someone inside by morning.
The farms survive because every drop of water has a place to go.
Smooth sandstone looks clean, though the lower courses take a beating from blown grit.
A bell needs open sightlines in a village where dust can hide the far houses.
I would ask which roof leaks before offering to rebuild anything.
Their paths may disappear under a single night's wind. Tall markers help more than curbs.
Keeping animals shaded is part of keeping the whole village fed.
Desert masons know how thick a wall must be before noon heat stays outside.
A cracked well rim deserves attention before any fancy new doorway.
Visitors should refill the water jars they empty.
At sunset, those pale houses hold the day's warmth longer than the open sand.
A village in that country lasts because everyone treats water and shade as shared work.
{target}? Open fields give little warning before danger arrives.
If anyone heads for Plains Village, tell them. Greet the bell and trade kindly.
Flat roads make visitors easy to see.
There is more to Plains Village than the maps suggest.
I'll remember Plains Village as neighbors with fields like ours.
Their roads are easy to follow, which means raiders can follow them too.
Cobblestone around the well keeps spring mud out of the water.
I'd check the farm walls first. Hooves and carts loosen the low courses.
Open fields let the bell carry from one end of the village to the other.
A sturdy porch matters when every neighbor stops to trade news.
The houses don't need to be grand if the roofs shed rain and the doors close square.
Farm paths wear into ruts after harvest. A few flat stones save a lot of ankles.
I would leave room for carts before adding any wall near the center.
Plains wind finds every loose shutter by nightfall.
Their iron golem can see far, but so can anyone watching the village.
A low boundary wall guides livestock without making neighbors feel penned in.
The best repair day is one when every household lends a pair of hands.
Hay belongs clear of chimneys, no matter how convenient the corner looks.
A bell square should stay open enough for frightened people to gather quickly.
Good foundations there are simple. Dig past the soft topsoil and set them level.
{target}? Dry grass carries sound and fire quickly.
If anyone heads for Savanna Village, tell them. Bring respect and watch the wind.
Acacia roofs know hard sun well.
You make Savanna Village sound beautiful from a safe distance.
I will remember Savanna Village as neighbors standing under a sharper sky.
Acacia beams hold well, though dry wind works every joint loose over time.
Their raised houses catch a breeze that the ground-level paths never feel.
I'd clear dead grass from every cooking fire before repairing a wall.
Orange roofs stand out across the plateau, which helps travelers find their way.
A stone apron around the well keeps dust and hoof marks away from the water.
Some paths climb sharply between houses. Steps need broad treads for loaded hands.
Shade from an acacia is welcome, but roots can lift a foundation block by block.
I would brace the windward wall before the next dry season.
Fire can cross that grass faster than a bell warning reaches the last house.
Their builders know how to leave air moving without letting the roof lift.
A village on uneven ground needs railings where children take the shortest route.
Cracked terracotta can often be replaced without disturbing the whole doorway.
Keep grain stores raised and dry when sudden rain runs off the hard soil.
A shared cistern would buy time when the well drops low.
The place feels open, but every roof and tree makes a pocket of useful shade.
{target}? Cold makes every chore heavier.
If anyone heads for Snowy Village, tell them. Shut doors fast and bring something warm.
Snow hides paths faster than gossip finds them.
There is more to Snowy Village than the maps suggest.
I will remember Snowy Village as neighbors keeping hearths alive in white country.
Snow loads a roof quietly. Someone has to clear it before the beams start complaining.
Their doors need sheltered steps or drifted snow seals them shut.
I'd repair a chimney before touching anything decorative in that cold.
Packed snow makes a good path until thaw turns the stones beneath it slick.
The well cover keeps both ice and careless boots out of the water.
A warm meeting house can matter more than several small rooms when a storm lasts days.
Foundations shift when frost gets into cracks and expands overnight.
I would mark the road with posts tall enough to stand above a fresh drift.
Spruce shutters keep wind out better when every hinge sits square.
Animals need thick walls too. A cold barn means an empty table later.
The bell rope should be reachable even when snow covers the square.
Roof edges need room to drop ice where nobody walks below.
A stone hearth stores heat long after the fire settles down.
Neighbors there check each other's chimneys because smoke can vanish in a blizzard.
Winter villages survive by fixing small gaps before the cold makes them large ones.
{target}? Trees and snow make quiet approaches easy.
If anyone heads for Taiga Village, tell them. Follow torchlight and respect their stores.
Spruce shadows can hide a lot.
I can see why people keep talking about Taiga Village after they leave.
I'll remember Taiga Village as neighbors tucked among cold trees.
Spruce roofs shed snow well if needles and moss aren't blocking the eaves.
Their paths twist between trunks, so torch posts matter after dark.
I'd set a stone footing under any wall built close to a wet forest floor.
Berry bushes belong away from doorways unless everyone likes scratched ankles.
A campfire roof needs a clear vent. Smoke settles low under thick branches.
Foxes find loose food stores faster than villagers notice a cracked latch.
The well path turns muddy each spring when the last snow melts.
I would trim roots away from a foundation without cutting the tree that holds the slope.
Spruce timber darkens with age, but sound wood still rings under a tap.
A bell can be hard to place where the forest swallows sightlines.
Stone steps help on shaded slopes that stay icy after the open ground thaws.
Their houses feel close together because the trees make every clearing precious.
A covered woodpile is nearly as important as a covered bed in winter.
I'd ask the hunters which trails flood before laying a new road.
That village stays hidden from distant trouble, though the same trees can hide trouble nearby.
{target}? Illagers make a house feel like a threat.
If anyone heads for Woodland Mansion, tell them. Don't enter alone, and do not trust the quiet rooms.
Dark oak walls can hold too many axes.
That tells me enough about Woodland Mansion to respect the place.
I will remember Woodland Mansion as a huge house that forgot how to be a home.
A repair at Woodland Mansion should leave the return route clearer than we found it.
If we camped at Woodland Mansion, I would put the entrance where the window side of the mansion stayed visible.
For Woodland Mansion, I would carry rubble for fill and dressed stone for the places taking weight.
I would clear loose rubble from the window side of the mansion before carrying anything heavy.
If we had to run, the window side of the mansion should already be marked and open.
No one should cross the hard part of Woodland Mansion without agreeing on the way back.
If our plan did not account for stairs opening onto danger, I would call it unfinished.
Any camp at Woodland Mansion needs to account for stairs opening onto danger before nightfall.
While moving through Woodland Mansion, I would keep one hand free and remember stairs opening onto danger.
I would tap the solid surfaces at Woodland Mansion and leave the hollow ones alone.
At Woodland Mansion, I would watch where loose pieces gather near the long dark hallways. They show where people slip.
The oldest damage at Woodland Mansion would be the first thing I measured.
I would leave the loot at Woodland Mansion if the window side of the mansion became unsafe.
I would share the load before asking anyone to hurry across the long dark hallways.
A missing tool is annoying. A missing traveler at Woodland Mansion is worse.
